title: The Flag Under Fire — Eddie Would Go

u.El 30 de enero de 2026, la Corte Suprema: On 30 January 2026, Panama's Supreme Court annulled CK Hutchison's concession over the ports of Balboa and Cristóbal. What followed was not a legal dispute. It was a calculated demonstration of how a power can turn the world's largest maritime registry into an instrument of geopolitical pressure. Seventy vessels detained. Forty per cent Japanese-owned. USD 270 billion of cargo at stake. This is the inventory of the reprisal.
u.«El control del mar mediante el comercio: «Control of the sea by maritime commerce and naval supremacy means predominant influence in the world.»
u.— Alfred Thayer Mahan, La Influencia del: — Alfred Thayer Mahan, The Influence of Sea Power upon History (1890)
u.En algún puerto de China, en algún momen: In some Chinese port, at some point between 8 March and the end of April 2026, a Japanese shipowner received word that his vessel was being held. The official reason: port state control inspection. The number of inspections of Panama-flagged vessels in Chinese ports had risen suddenly, systematically and, according to the United States maritime regulator, to levels that "greatly exceed historical norms". The Japanese shipowner had taken no part in any decision about the Panama Canal. His company had no relationship with CK Hutchison, or BlackRock, or the Mulino government. He had simply chosen to register his vessel in Panama, as 15% of the world's ships do. That choice, which is routinely commercial, had become a geopolitical variable.
u.Lo que pasó en el Canal de Panamá entre: What happened in the Panama Canal between January and May 2026 has a technical name in international law: state economic coercion. It also has a precise mechanism: the weaponisation of a maritime registry. And it has a dimension the usual debate about the Canal systematically omits: it is not only a dispute between Washington and Beijing. It is the story of how Panama, a country of 4.4 million people, became the battlefield of the greatest strategic rivalry of the twenty-first century.
u.I. EL FALLO QUE CAMBIÓ TODO: I. THE RULING THAT CHANGED EVERYTHING
u.La concesión de CK Hutchison sobre los t: CK Hutchison's concession over the Balboa and Cristóbal terminals dates from 1997. Almost three decades of uninterrupted operation at the two ends of the canal —one on the Pacific, the other on the Atlantic— made the Hong Kong company the most important private operator of Panamanian port infrastructure. The concession was, for all practical purposes, part of the canal's institutional landscape.
u.El 30 de enero de 2026, la Corte Suprema: On 30 January 2026, Panama's Supreme Court declared it unconstitutional. The ruling followed an audit that detected irregularities in the original concession process and questioned its legal framework. The Mulino government, which had spent all of 2025 resisting American pressure to review the Chinese presence in the canal, now had a judicial ruling authorising it to act —and a relationship with Washington that had deteriorated enough for the action to be a diplomatic signal as well.
u.La transición fue rápida. El 23 de enero: The transition was rapid. On 23 January, before the definitive ruling, the government assumed control of both facilities citing "urgent social interest" and the need to guarantee operational continuity. Maersk, through its subsidiary APM Terminals, took Balboa. MSC, through Terminal Investment Limited, took Cristóbal. Eighteen-month contracts. The contract value for Balboa alone: USD 26.1 million, according to documents cited by La Estrella de Panamá. The transition had an immediate winner: Maersk, which already handled between 75 and 80% of container traffic at Balboa, was positioned as favourite for the permanent tender process the Panamanian Maritime Authority announced for the transition period.
u.Para CK Hutchison, la consecuencia fue i: For CK Hutchison, the consequence was immediate: the company launched international arbitration against the government of Panama. The amount claimed exceeds USD 2 billion. The argument: "unlawful taking" of its port assets. The arbitration process may drag on for years and the outcome is uncertain. What is not uncertain is that Panama Ports Company —the subsidiary that operated the ports— lost access to its facilities before any international tribunal had ruled.
u.II. EL CÁLCULO QUE SE ROMPIÓ: PANAMÁ Y E: II. THE CALCULATION THAT BROKE: PANAMA AND THE BRI (2017–2025)
u.Lo que pasó en el Canal de Panamá no emp: What happened in the Panama Canal did not begin in January 2026. It began in November 2017, when Panama became the first country in Latin America to formally join China's Belt and Road Initiative — the BRI. It was a moment of geopolitical audacity for a small country that believed it could navigate between the two powers without picking a side. Eight years later, that calculation is completely broken.
u.El 3 de febrero de 2025, el día de la vi: On 3 February 2025, the day of Rubio's visit to the canal, the Mulino government announced that Panama would not renew its participation in the BRI. On 6 February, it formalised the notification with 90 days' notice. Panama thus became the first Latin American country both to join and to withdraw from the BRI — a complete arc of alignment, reversal and consequences without precedent in the region. Mulino's response when asked what the BRI had brought the country: he did not know what to say.
u.Analistas del CSIS bautizaron a esta sec: Analysts at CSIS christened this sequence —exit from the BRI, judicial annulment of the concession, increasingly explicit alignment with Washington— the “Mulino Doctrine”: a strategy of autonomy through institutional and legal mechanisms, not through military alignment or ideological rhetoric. The piece that doctrine still needs to complete itself is already under way: in parallel with the BRI exit, the Mulino government signed a security cooperation memorandum with the Pentagon. In the eighteen months since he took office, in July 2024, Panama went from trying to navigate between the two powers without choosing a side to building, piece by piece, a legal and institutional file documenting exactly the opposite.
u.Los números revelan la asimetría que sub: The numbers reveal the asymmetry underlying the whole relationship. In 2023, Chinese direct investment in Panama represented 0.8% of the total. American investment: 19.6%. Spain contributed 3.6%. China was never the dominant partner in terms of capital. But it was the visible partner — the one that had signed the infrastructure agreements, that operated the ports, that supplied the narrative framework of South-South cooperation. When Trump needed an argument to pressure Panama, that visibility was enough.
u.El patrón que Panamá ilustra no es exclu: The pattern Panama illustrates is not unique. Brazil never formally joined the BRI, despite Chinese pressure. Colombia went as far as considering it and withdrew. Italy, the only G7 country that had entered, abandoned it in December 2023 under American pressure, arguing that it had brought no concrete economic benefits. According to The Conversation's analysis, more than 20 countries in Latin America and the Caribbean maintain formal BRI membership — but the region is watching what happened to Panama. The question each of those governments is now asking itself is simple: how much does it cost to leave, and how much does it cost to stay?
u.La respuesta que Panamá está dando en ti: The answer Panama is giving in real time is unsettling for both questions. The cost of leaving was immediate: seventy vessels detained, COSCO suspended, Maersk and MSC summoned to Beijing, and a USD 2 billion arbitration under way. The cost of staying would have been different — American pressure on a country that depends on Washington for its security, its currency and most of its foreign investment was not sustainable indefinitely. Panama did not choose its position in this conflict. Its position — interoceanic canal, global maritime registry, crossroads of trade routes — chose it.
u.El documento de Estrategia de Defensa Na: The United States National Defense Strategy document published in January 2026 confirms that this is not an incident. It is a policy. The document, according to the China-Global South Project, confirms that a strategic shift is under way in the Western Hemisphere. The question that shift leaves for the 20 Latin American countries that still have BRI agreements in force is the same one Mulino could not answer when asked what the BRI had brought Panama. Some will have a different answer. The cost-benefit model they will use to calculate it already has a test case: what happened after Panama broke with Beijing, when the diplomatic rupture became a judicial ruling, and the judicial ruling became a reprisal calculated on three fronts.
u.III. LA REPRESALIA EN TRES FRENTES: III. THE REPRISAL ON THREE FRONTS
u.La respuesta china fue coordinada, rápid: The Chinese response was coordinated, rapid and multidimensional. It did not come from a single ministry or through a single channel. It came simultaneously from the state transport system, from commercial diplomacy and from port control mechanisms —which in China are an instrument of foreign policy when the government decides they are.
u.El primer frente fue COSCO. El cuarto ma: The first front was COSCO. The world's fourth largest container carrier, Chinese state-owned, suspended its services at the Balboa terminal fifteen days after Maersk and MSC took control. The decision is as much strategic signal as real logistical impact: according to La Prensa data, Maersk already handled the bulk of traffic at Balboa, so COSCO's absence does not paralyse the terminal. But the image is deliberate. COSCO redirected part of its transhipment activity towards the Colombian port of Buenaventura, on the Pacific, introducing Colombia as an indirect recipient of the conflict.
u.El segundo frente fue la convocatoria di: The second front was the diplomatic summons. The Chinese Ministry of Transport called in executives from Maersk and MSC for "high-level discussions on international shipping operations". In Chinese regulatory language, that kind of summons is not an invitation to debate. It is a signal that the state considers those companies' commercial conduct to be under scrutiny in sectors deemed vital to national trade. The United States Federal Maritime Commission publicly recorded the summonses in its March statement.
u.El tercer frente es el más sofisticado y: The third front is the most sophisticated and the one with the greatest systemic impact: the wave of port state control inspections of Panama-flagged vessels. The formal mechanism exists in international maritime law —states have the right to inspect foreign vessels in their ports to verify compliance with safety and environmental standards. What does not exist in international law is the use of that mechanism as coordinated political reprisal. That is exactly what the FMC documented: informal directives, a detention frequency far above the historical norm, and a temporal pattern coinciding with the transfer of the Hutchison assets.
u.Los números detrás de esa oleada, recons: The numbers behind that wave, reconstructed from Tokyo MOU data —the port state control authority for the Asia-Pacific region— show a curve the average of “seventy vessels” fails to convey. In January 2026, 23 of the vessels detained in Chinese ports flew the Panamanian flag; in February, 20. In March, the month of the break, the figure jumped to 92: almost three quarters of all detentions recorded in China that month. In April it reached 135. In May, 139. The total for those two months —274— exceeded all Panama-flagged detentions recorded in the whole of 2025. Only in June, with 64 detentions, did the figure fall 54% against May: the first sign that something was beginning to ease. Beijing, for its part, offers a different explanation: the Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman, Guo Jiakun, attributed the rise in inspections to a series of collisions involving Panama-flagged vessels in Chinese waters during 2026, and maintains that this is a matter of maritime safety, not political reprisal. The problem for that version is the calendar: the collisions do not explain why the detention curve spikes on exactly 8 March, fourteen days after Maersk and MSC took control of Balboa and Cristóbal, nor why it halves as soon as a Panamanian diplomatic mission to Beijing is announced.
u.Setenta buques detenidos desde el 8 de m: Seventy vessels detained since 8 March. Informal directives. A frequency far above the historical norm. The United States maritime regulator left no doubt about the nature of the measure.
u.IV. LA BANDERA MÁS CASTIGADA DEL MUNDO: IV. THE MOST PUNISHED FLAG IN THE WORLD
u.Para entender el alcance del daño, hay q: To understand the scope of the damage, one has to understand what the Panamanian maritime registry is. Panama has the largest flag fleet in the world: more than 4,700 cargo and container vessels representing around 15% of global tonnage. But most of those ships are not Panamanian in any operational sense. They are vessels belonging to European, Japanese, Greek, Korean, Taiwanese and American owners who chose the Panamanian registry for its commercial advantages: competitive fees, regulatory flexibility, historic political neutrality.
u.Esa neutralidad histórica es exactamente: That historic neutrality is exactly what China eliminated in March 2026. By applying pressure on the Panamanian flag as a mechanism of reprisal, Beijing turned a maritime registration decision —which is essentially administrative and commercial— into a political statement. And the shipowners who have nothing to do with the canal dispute paid the cost.
u.El dato que captura mejor la magnitud de: The figure that best captures the magnitude of the collateral damage was produced by Lloyd's List: of the nearly 70 vessels detained in Chinese ports since 8 March, 39% are Japanese-owned. Tokyo took no decision about the Panama Canal. Japanese shipping companies were not among the substitute operators for CK Hutchison. Yet their vessels spent weeks in Chinese ports under "port state control inspections" while their cargoes waited and their operating costs mounted. Flag reprisal produces collateral damage without discrimination.
u.El costo no se mide solo en buques deten: The cost is not measured only in vessels detained: it is measured in vessels that leave. According to Lloyd's List Intelligence data, 180 vessels abandoned the Panamanian flag in May 2026; in June, 264 —a 47% jump— with the Bahamas and the Marshall Islands receiving more than half of those registry transfers. The most uncomfortable fact for Beijing sits inside that figure: the group of owners that withdrew the most vessels from the Panamanian flag in June was, precisely, of Chinese origin —fifty linked to mainland China, twenty to Hong Kong.
u.China castiga la bandera panameña con in: China punishes the Panamanian flag with inspections and, at the same time, its own shipowners abandon it, which suggests that commercial calculation has already begun to outweigh political loyalty. The medium-term consequence is regulatory: if the detention rate holds, Panama risks falling from the white list to the grey list in international port state control rankings —a downgrade that would make the registry more expensive for every shipowner who decides to stay, regardless of how the political conflict ends.
u.Panamá ya empezó a cortejar activamente: Panama has already begun actively courting a replacement: in 2025 and 2026, Mulino received at the Palacio de las Garzas both Keidanren, the Japanese business federation, and the Japanese shipowners' association, offering to modernise the maritime registry and adding an interoceanic gas pipeline and a reservoir at Río Indio to the table as incentives. Japan, the principal collateral victim of the Chinese detentions, is also the partner Panama is courting to replace the centrality China once had.
u.Para la industria naviera global, el pre: For the global shipping industry, the precedent is disturbing. If a country's flag can become the target of reprisal for its government's decisions on port concessions, the calculus of maritime registration changes. Shipowners can no longer treat the choice of flag as a purely commercial decision. They have to assess whether the country of registry has stable diplomatic relations with the principal destination ports of their cargo. David Smith, of the University of Sydney's US Studies Centre, summed it up precisely to Al Jazeera: "We have taken for granted that the world works with container ships sailing freely around the world". The Panama conflict demonstrated that this assumption is not universal.
u.V. LA ARITMÉTICA QUE NADIE PUEDE IGNORAR: V. THE ARITHMETIC NOBODY CAN IGNORE
u.El Canal de Panamá no es una disputa ent: The Panama Canal is not a dispute between two countries. It is the most important infrastructure dispute in the Western Hemisphere. The numbers explain why.
u.El 40% de todo el tráfico de contenedore: Forty per cent of all United States container traffic transits the canal annually. In total the canal moves around USD 270 billion of cargo a year. The Panama Canal Authority has transferred approximately USD 31.2 billion to the Panamanian National Treasury since the country assumed control in 1999 —which makes the canal the most important fiscal asset of the Panamanian state. And the ACP's 2025–2035 strategic plan projects USD 8.5 billion in investment to maintain the competitiveness of the interoceanic waterway and its associated logistics infrastructure.
u.Para China, el canal tiene otra dimensió: For China, the canal has another dimension. Any expansion of Chinese maritime dominance in the zone, according to the Foundation for Defense of Democracies cited by CNBC, could put the US and its allies at risk of the same dependence they face with critical minerals and rare earths. The American reasoning that justified the pressure on Panama was not only ideological —it was logistical. If COSCO or other Chinese state companies control the two entry terminals to the canal, they have the theoretical capacity to create operational friction over 40% of US container trade at any moment of tension.
u.La respuesta de Mulino, al presentar el: Mulino's response, in presenting the close of 2025 as the end of the crisis with Washington, underestimates the complexity of what is coming. The canal can remain sovereignly Panamanian —and it is— and at the same time be the stage for a competition of power Panama does not control. The terminals go to permanent tender. COSCO is interested in taking part. China already blocked the sale of CK Hutchison to the BlackRock consortium unless it included a majority stake for COSCO. The tender process will be the next chapter of this conflict.
u.En abril de 2026, mientras la tensión so: In April 2026, while tension over the Panamanian vessels remained active, China approved a series of new rules allowing the state to retaliate against measures adopted outside its territory that affect its interests. The extraterritorial countermeasures law —which has existed since 2021 but was updated— now provides a domestic legal framework for actions such as the inspections of Panama-flagged vessels. What was informal pressure now has regulatory backing.
u.El arbitraje de CK Hutchison, que busca: The CK Hutchison arbitration, seeking more than USD 2 billion, may take between three and five years. In that time, the Balboa and Cristóbal terminals will go through an international tender process. Bolivia, Costa Rica, Guyana, Paraguay, Trinidad and Tobago and the US issued a joint declaration in April 2026 criticising China's "selective economic pressure" on Panamanian vessels —an unusual coalition that signals the level of regional alarm at the precedent.
u.La pregunta que el conflicto del canal d: The question the canal conflict leaves open is not about Panama. It is about the system. If China can respond to another state's sovereign judicial ruling with the systematic detention of vessels registered in that state —affecting shipowners from third countries with no role in the conflict— then the framework of rules supposed to order global maritime trade works differently from what was believed. It is not broken. But nor is it universal. It is conditional on no sufficiently large power deciding that the conditions have changed.
u.La escalada no se detuvo con la temporad: The escalation did not stop with the season of detentions. The United States Federal Maritime Commission is weighing a formal investigation into what its chairman describes as China's “weaponisation” of port control —a step that would raise the conflict from diplomatic monitoring to formal regulatory proceeding. Behind that threat a clock is running: the punitive port fees Washington and Beijing imposed on each other's vessels are suspended, but they expire in November 2026, and could be reactivated if the broader trade negotiations between the two powers break down —which would turn the Panama dispute into one more front of a trade war already under way, rather than an isolated conflict. Meanwhile, and probably not by coincidence, Panama sent an official delegation to Beijing between 16 and 18 July 2026 to renegotiate the bilateral Maritime Transport Agreement —in force since 2017— and to discuss the inspection regime directly. The 54% fall in June detentions suggests both sides came to that table looking to lower the temperature, not raise it. But neither Washington nor Beijing gave any sign of yielding on the structural question: who controls, in practice, the two ends of the canal remains unanswered.
u.Mahan escribió en 1890 que el control de: Mahan wrote in 1890 that control of the sea meant predominant influence in the world. What the Panama Canal is demonstrating in 2026 is that the proposition remains true —and that the instruments for exercising that control are no longer only naval. They are maritime registries, ministerial summonses, port inspections and USD 2 billion arbitrations. Sea power in the twenty-first century does not arrive with cannon. It arrives with bureaucracy.
